question: In its judgements Dano (C‑333/13) and Alimanovic (C‑67/14), the Court of Justice of the European Union acknowledged that economically inactive EU citizens can be excluded from social benefits under certain conditions. 1.

Does the Commission hold the view that Member States may differentiate between economically active and economically inactive EU citizens when granting access to certain family-related social benefits?
What criteria does the Commission consider particularly relevant when assessing such a differentiation under EU law?
To what extent does the Commission consider protecting the financial viability of national social benefit systems to be a legitimate aim under EU law?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (10.7.2026) As stated by the Court of Justice in Dano1, Member States may exclude from social assistance economically inactive nationals of other Member States who – due to insufficient resources – do not fulfil the conditions for residence based on Directive 2004/38/EC.

In Commission v UK2, the Court stated that Member States may require economically inactive mobile EU citizens to reside lawfully in their territory based on Directive 2004/38/EC to receive noncontributory family related social benefits falling into the scope of Article 1(z) of Regulation (EC) No 883/2004.

In addition, pursuant to Article 24(2) of Directive 2004/38/EC, Member States may limit for certain periods the entitlement to social assistance and maintenance aid referred to in that provision of mobile EU citizens who are not economically active.

By contrast, mobile EU citizens who are workers or who are self-employed persons (or those who retain that status following the cessation of an economic activity3) and their family members are entitled to the same social assistance as nationals from the beginning of their stay4.

As also mentioned by the Court in Dano5, the exclusion of economically inactive citizens who are not residing lawfully in their territory based on the Directive 2004/38/EC from equal access to social assistance is intended to prevent such EU citizens from using the host Member State’s welfare system to fund their means of subsistence and to ensure that no unreasonable burden is placed on the social assistance systems of the host Member State.

1 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 11 November 2014, Dano, C-333/13, EU:C:2014:2358, paragraph 82. 2 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 16 June 2016, Commission v UK, C-308/14, ECLI:EU:C:2016:436,

paragraph 86. 3 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 15 September 2015, Alimanovic, C-67/14, ECLI:EU:C:2015:597, paragraphs 53 and 54. 4 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 25 February 2016, García-Nieto, C-299/14, ECLI:EU:C:2016:114, paragraph 44. 5 Judgment of the Court of Justice of 11 November 2014, Dano, C-333/13, EU:C:2014:2358, paragraphs 74 and 76.
